label: Slow CI reuses one worktree and keeps its build tree between runs
The fast check fits its lanes into 60 s and stops a step at 180 s
Heavy commands take CPU tokens from one pool shared by the whole machine
The Rust tests step takes CPU tokens freed after it starts
Slow-CI runs start at least five minutes apart
The fast Rust lane checks only the crates a change reaches
Rust tests build at opt-level 1
New worktrees keep cargo's view of unchanged files
Full browser sweeps move from slow CI to a run every three hours
The oracle lane plays only scenarios new to the oracles
Beryl 3D's tests, record and gate share one test-profile build, with one integration-test binary per crate
Beryl 3D's tuning and corpus checks use the shared build
Only beryl_3d and beryl_record link the engine, so an engine edit rebuilds no other Beryl 3D test
The Beryl 3D instruction-count gate counts every frame in one Callgrind run per board, and no bead waits for it before pushing
Every worktree reuses one of ten slot directories, keeping rustc's incremental caches
Clippy builds in its own target directory, and the steps that run beryl_cli share one build before taking CPU tokens
Concurrent ui-test runs keep separate fixture recordings so they do not retry checks after deleting each other's files
Every cargo command, typed or started by `by`, takes CPU tokens and grows its build as tokens come free
Beryl 3D trees clone the cached build directory once, and sweep and coverage trees reuse one path
Lima VMs hold CPU tokens for their cores, run in the background for low-priority work, and stop after 15 idle minutes
Beryl 3D's saved build cache and worktree build directories are held to the 15 GB budget, so each clone copies one build instead of every earlier one
A rebase merges data/beryl3d/gates.json's limits as numbers instead of stopping on a conflict, and a new worktree's Beryl 3D build reuses the cached build instead of rebuilding every crate
The fast check's Beryl 3D steps run in four lanes at once, with clippy in its own target and builds waiting without tokens
Beryl 3D's export command writes the recordings on as many threads as its CPU tokens allow

Every six hours each worktree's rust/target and rust/beryl3d/target delete the builds that newer builds of the same units replaced, deleting them in the background, so a reused slot holds one build instead of a day's worth
Agents send their file reads and searches in one message instead of one request per read, and beads name files by path so a session can read them all at once
Beryl 3D timeline parity reuses the shared build for export and timeline playback
Sweep step replays skip the sweep's lock, and waited-for runs go first on the bench VM
The fast check's Beryl 3D interface tests run the b3d of the shared build instead of building b3d alone, so the cargo-test and timeline-parity lanes no longer wait behind that build
Each fast-check lane reads per-hour and per-day sums of the run log instead of scanning the whole 1.4 GB file twice, so choosing and timing its checks takes under half a second

An agent's cargo build gives its spare CPU tokens back while a push waits, and a push that would start short waits up to 10 s for them, so a push's fast-check steps stop running on one core beside long agent builds

A flaky check files its delete bead only when it flakes again in another run within a week, so one-off problems of a run (load, a shared fixture, code changing between attempts) no longer start an Opus session each
A Beryl 3D program in a fast check (record, b3d test) takes more CPU tokens while it runs as other steps release them, and adds threads, instead of keeping the one to three tokens it started with
Beryl 3D reuses placement lookups while compiling scripts and visits fewer effects for each card
Beryl 3D's fast-check cargo-test runs only the tests that fit the time left
Single-threaded b3d commands take one CPU token instead of twelve
An agent's cargo build starts at once on the CPU tokens that are free and grows as slow CI and the sweeps give theirs back, instead of waiting up to 10 s for them

The commands `just b3d tree`, `png` and `film` start their rebuild without waiting for CPU tokens, run their one-thread program outside the pool, and build `dev` without ThinLTO, so a one-line edit to `beryl_scene` shows in about 3 s instead of 4 to 127 s

The fast check's Beryl 3D cargo-test step runs its tests in waves when its CPU lease got fewer tokens than it wanted, taking the tokens that free up before each wave, instead of running every test on the 1-2 threads it started with (60-115 s on one thread against 18-25 s on twelve)

Push and queue cargo builds, and growing programs such as Beryl 3D's record, start at once on the CPU tokens that are free and hold lower classes back while they grow, instead of waiting up to 10 s for elastic tokens before a build or record that usually has nothing to do
Beryl 3D's fast-check test steps stop at the run's target, after at least 45 s of tests, instead of filling the time up to the 180 s hard limit
Card writers can omit hand-written scenarios when generated scenarios cover every mutant and pass the oracle check

A push's fast check runs in one of three reused check trees, check-1 to check-3, which stay a commit or two behind staging and keep their rustc incremental caches, instead of in the pushing tree, which rebuilt every crate staging changed since its agent started (Beryl 3D shared test build: median 134 CPU-seconds per push)
Card writers start from a Rust draft and see vocabulary and example files only for unresolved clauses

The fast check's pytest step runs the Python test files that fit its window, those the change edits or whose imports reach it first, and stops at the window's end, instead of all 855 tests on any tools/ change (median 93 s, cut off at 180 s in a quarter of runs), and the browser sweep runs the whole suite

A flaky-check bead and its repeat comments quote the failed attempt's output, kept for 14 days in $BERYL_CACHE/ci/flakes, instead of naming only the step and sending an Opus session to look for logs that the rerun and the Beryl 3D sweep had already overwritten (6 such beads for whole steps open on 2026-11-17)

The `just b3d timeline-parity` command names Beryl 3D's timeline file by nanosecond and process id, and writes the web timeline cache by rename, so the Beryl 3D sweep's timeline-parity and timeline-parity-all steps, which run at once and share $BERYL_CACHE/b3d, no longer delete or half-read each other's files (the cause behind flaky-check beads by-o3wua and by-s9etj)

A nightly-failure bead quotes its own step's output and names a file that keeps it for two weeks, instead of the tail of the whole night (which ended with the oracle and iroh steps) in a file the next firing overwrote, so a Steward no longer re-runs a 2-10 minute `just fuzz` just to see what failed
Enact replaces local sync and its 4.7 s median ownership-lock wait with tk coordination
Enact tk documents every option, provides offline agent guidance and supports --brief discovery output so sessions avoid loading full ticket bodies to select work
Beryl 3D's record command runs the linker's executable so warm builds reuse its macOS first-run validation instead of launching Cargo's refreshed copy
Oracle outcomes use each scenario’s exported inputs so unrelated exporter edits retain prior passes
Native builds avoid stale LLVM-symbol links and manual cleans by disabling incremental reuse only for dependencies, while native workspace edits remain incremental

Python tests that run a fake ui-test, shots, script or oracle lane no longer start the real workspace cargo build from inside pytest, where four tests spent 37-59 s each in it, about 190 test-seconds and 500 CPU-seconds per full run in a fresh worktree

Beryl 3D's parity-list check runs in the fast check's repo lane on every change instead of only in the 3-hourly Beryl 3D sweep, so a deleted or added skill fails at push time rather than leaving the sweep red, re-bisected and re-commented every run until a session takes the ticket

The switch from Enact to Ignite: Ignite builds, checks and lands every change and holds the tickets, with checks chosen by input hashes, a shared result cache and scores in place of Enact's fast check, slow CI, sweeps, nightly, CPU token pool and role files
Tip verification lists each family once per round, runs families in parallel landing trees, builds the whole workspace when a subset's features differ, and leaves a waiting tip for ten minutes
Kept listings (memory, local, hub) and the landing gate deciding which families a change can affect before it lists or builds anything
Tip claims sized by measured cost instead of 50 checks, and a covered family (b3d-interface) not run beside the family that covers it
Two budgets: the gate runs 60 s of checks at the landing rate on what its tree has already built, leaving checks that need a cold build to tip verification
Two budgets: master moves after 300 s of the best-scored tip checks, the rest running after it moves
Running `just b3d cargo-test -p` filters the shared workspace build instead of building the named crates again: 74 crates and 689 CPU-s (310 s wall) after the shared build, now 0 crates and 1 CPU-s
Compiling grants give cores back to waiters of their own class past a fair share: 15 agent requests had queued 148-164 s behind one 12-core build
Tree sweep keeps every unit a kept build reaches (it deleted 35 live build-script runs of 23 crates in one tree), and compiling tickets prefer a tree holding the build directory beside their files

Quick commands (last 5+ runs each under 2 CPU-s, not Cargo) start without waiting for a core: `uv sync` for the Python environment used at most 1.2 CPU-s but queued up to 726 s before listing any family
Grants whose commands leave cores idle lend them to waiting requests: every core was granted for an hour while the machine stayed half idle and requests queued
Landings that change only Ignite run its fmt, clippy and tests on reserved cores in a fixed warm tree instead of the gate: four Ignite fixes waited 10 to 30 minutes in the scheduler they were fixing

A landing that loses the race for the tip keeps its landing tree and re-gates only the families the commits landed since touch: before, each lost race re-ran the whole gate, often in another tree that built again (2-pass landings took 28 minutes against 7 for one pass)
The Rust adapter imports the card modules only for the card-text family, and `allocations` lists without a build: a comment edited in card.py made a landing wait 40 minutes on a cold rust-tests build

The daemon's launchd agent is Interactive: under Standard every Ignite command ran at utility priority on the slower cores, doing half the work per CPU-second while load reached 53 with 56% of the CPU idle

A compiling lease starts from an APFS copy of the build of the tree nearest the tip: in a second tree the cli, test-binary and release fuzz-test builds took 5.4, 6.3 and 0.2 CPU-s, against cold medians of 947, 1,070 and 1,390 CPU-s

A change confined to the express paths judges a family with no kept listing by its declared inputs: a change touching only Ignite's files selected 637 checks, built `b3d` (310 CPU-s) and gated twice, about 95 s each

Ignite's own tests run under cargo-nextest, from the test build, and fmt and clippy no longer wait for that build: warm on 2026-11-18 at load 30 to 43 the 1325 tests took 13.2 s wall and 59 CPU-s against 35 s and 91 CPU-s through `cargo test`, which ran the 29 test binaries one after another, and clippy re-checked the workspace in about 4 s

The monitor rewrites a daemon launchd agent an older build wrote: hours after the agent became Interactive, jarvis still ran every rustc at utility priority, ten of them at a quarter core each with 40% of the CPU idle, because only `ignite install` wrote the agent

Both `ignite test` of Ignite's own checks and `ignite check` run the express commands on the reserved express cores when the tree changes only Ignite: through the scheduler they took 5 to 8.5 minutes while other builds held its cores, against 40 s warm on 3 express cores after a daemon edit (fmt 0 s, clippy 2 s, nextest 38 s)

The Claude dispatcher's settings deny the tools its loop never calls, which Claude Code then leaves out of its context: the desktop app's browser, simulator, chart, terminal and editing tools took about 60,000 of its 120,000-token window before its first message, so each request re-sent them and it compacted after about 27,000 tokens of loop

Ignite's release build is incremental and its dev and test profiles keep only line tables: after a daemon-only edit the release rebuild took 75 s on 3 cores and now takes about 4 s, and the express commands (clippy, test build and nextest run) took 85 s and now take about 70 s

Beryl's `.claude/settings.json` denies tools that 1,737 sessions over 14 days called at most twice (Artifact, Workflow, the built-in browser pane and Chrome, the iOS simulator, charts, plugin suggestions, the app's panes and pull requests), and Claude Code leaves a denied tool out of every request's context

The scheduler counts the daemon's whole process tree, express runs included, as Ignite's and reads the busy fraction against all logical cores: it reported 8 to 11 cores busy outside Ignite while outside processes used 3.5 to 4, and held those cores back

An express landing skips the express commands when the same git tree passed them within the hour, as when `ignite land` follows `ignite check` at an unmoved tip: jarvis ran 17 express checks averaging 213 s beside 30 landings on 2026-11-18, so each Ignite change paid for the three-core lane twice
Express runs borrow the scheduler's idle cores, up to 12 in all, instead of always running on the 3 reserved ones (about 164 s on 3 cores under load against about 65 s on 12)

A daemon restarts into a new release only after 90 s with no newer release, at most 10 minutes after the first: on 2026-11-18 jarvis's daemon restarted 16 times in 103 minutes, once per Ignite landing, and each restart reran every `ignite start` in progress
The fuzz, exhaust and app families list without waiting for their release test builds and `npm ci`, which their lists never read

The command `ignite land` runs the formatters of `[format]` on the changed files and commits what they change before its checks, and a failed express clippy names `cargo clippy -p <crate>` to run locally: on 2026-11-18 formatting and clippy failures found one Ignite round trip at a time cost one epic's workers about 25 minutes

The command `ignite test` looks a bare name up in each family's newest listing, so a one-card change no longer lists and builds every family (ignite test oust took 39 minutes and 816 s of builds in 8 products, and a full-gate ignite check of the same change took 229 s, and of a second card change 44 s, under full load on 2026-11-19)

An express landing reuses its tree's `ignite check` pass when the commits landed since touch none of the change's files or build inputs: on 2026-11-18 a landing reran all four express commands (56 s) a minute after its check had passed them in 60 s, because a commit had landed meanwhile

The command `ignite start` replies before a compiling tree's build directories are copied from another tree, and the copy runs on the prebuild thread and builds in the tree wait for it (9 of 25 starts between 05:38 and 06:38 UTC on 2026-11-19 had waited 30 to 141 s for the copy)

An express pass from `ignite test` in a tree with uncommitted edits is remembered by the tree ID of the files on disk, so the landing reuses it once exactly those edits are committed: on 2026-11-19 two Ignite fixes reran the express commands after a passing `ignite test`, waiting 220 s and 379 s

The dispatcher's release frees a tree leased under an ad hoc placeholder that no `ignite start` claimed before a daemon restart, and the dispatcher answers `gone` for an archived session: on 2026-11-19 about 95 of the Claude dispatcher's 426 instructions were reminders to three archived sessions whose trees the hub could not release, one every 15 minutes for up to 9 hours

The dispatcher's stall watch keeps a record of every check, so a worker answered `running`, or one whose release failed, is checked again only after another 30 minutes of silence, and a worker whose ticket just ended settles 3 minutes before its next hand-off, and on 2026-11-19, from 04:00 to 14:30, the Claude dispatcher received about 44 instructions an hour, 231 of them `check`s: 30 repeated `running` checks of one worker in 4 minutes, and two checks plus a reminder every 15 minutes for each worker whose release failed, and 32 of its 114 hand-offs failed because the app refused to clear a session still finishing its turn

The Claude dispatcher runs `ignite dispatch --wait 3600` as a background command instead of an 8-minute foreground wait, so it wakes once an hour when there is nothing to do instead of about 7 times, and on 2026-11-19 197 of its 426 instructions were `idle` wake-ups, each a full request over its context, and the daemon now keeps only the newest wait from each dispatcher, so a second wait started after a worker's notice is harmless

A daemon restarts into a new release 15 s after the last release appeared instead of 90 s, and the restart still waits while any landing runs or a newer release builds, which already merges releases landing one after another, and on 2026-11-19 a lone Ignite landing's `ignite wait deploy-<commit>` took 100 to 116 s, of which the build was about 40 s and the rest the 90 s quiet window

The `ignite` check family hashes each test over its own crate's dependency closure (`crate-closure`) instead of all of `ignite/`, so a landing that edits a check manifest under ignite/checks/, or that rebases over another landing's Ignite change, reruns only the tests whose crates changed instead of all 1562, and on 2026-11-19 a Beryl 3D change that edited beryl3d.toml ran the whole workspace's tests on each of four landing passes, 40 to 200 s each

A landing whose gate fails only on checks that also fail at the tip it was rebased onto lands with them known to fail and has their regression filed at once, instead of waiting unlanded until someone fixes the tip, as a Beryl 3D change did on 2026-11-19 behind 28 findings an earlier landing had introduced

Workers start `ignite land`, `check`, `test` and `wait` in the background and end the turn instead of sleep-polling or holding a foreground call to the 600 s Bash limit, and the post-start title reminder lets the title call share a request with the first reads (on 2026-11-19, 33 worker sessions spent 151 minutes in 108 sleep-poll calls, and 45 `ignite` calls ran 530 to 601 s in the foreground)

Ignite release builds and selftests run on the express cores instead of queueing for the scheduler's, the daemon notices a landing's release move at the next sender round instead of its five-minute fetch, and the restart cap is 30 s instead of 600 s (on 2026-11-19 the median release reached jarvis 395 s after its landing moved it)

The `rust` check family hashes each test over the repository files its build was observed to read, from Cargo's dep-info files and build-script outputs, instead of eleven hand-listed data paths that every test hashed, so an edit to the table commands or the save breaks reruns only the tests of the packages that embed them, and an edit to the card store or UI conventions reruns only the packages that depend on the embedding crate or read the file at run time, instead of all of the workspace's tests

The gate scores checks of families listed under Ignite from their recorded costs instead of as never run at one billion instructions, and b3d-clippy is in the always set only for changes to Beryl 3D (a one-card comment change's gate C-1642 ran 656 s of checks, 369 s of them two allocations checks planned at 2 billion that cost 3,041, and 216 s b3d-clippy)

The express lane's nextest profile leaves out Ignite's ten tests over 3 s, which tip verification still runs, and `ignite_cli`'s eight integration-test binaries are one, and the express test run uses a thread per core, so its test run after a daemon edit takes 12 to 17 s instead of 56 to 96 s at a load average of about 20

Rust test listings compile nothing on a built tree, and a game change no longer lists Ignite's test family (on 2026-11-19 most `rust` listings spent 18 to 25 s recompiling `beryl-mobile` and `beryl_app`)

A seeded tree copies the build of the donor that never built the fewest products and differs from the tip in the fewest files, instead of the one nearest by commits, which after a one-card change left 85 crates to rebuild for Beryl 3D and 98 for clippy

An `ignite land` after a passing `ignite check` of the same change charges its budget for the checks the check chose, now cached, so it runs no second slice of scored checks (on 2026-11-19 such a land of a one-line comment ran 398 more checks in 173 s), and the gate converts its seconds at the rate its own gates achieved in the last hour, so a 60 s budget runs in about 60 s under load

An express landing names its rebased commit as the release candidate and the daemon builds that release while the landing runs its express commands, the sender loop starts a round as soon as the release moves or its build ends instead of every 10 s, the restart's quiet window is 5 s instead of 15, and express `ignite test` and `ignite check` run the formatters first instead of failing on `cargo fmt --check` or mdformat (on 2026-11-19 two Ignite-only fixes waited 45 to 47 s from landing to restart, 36 s of it the release build, and lost a round trip each to formatting)

The `ignite test` command lists and runs its families on threads of their own, so their products build at once, and names every step of 5 s or more (on 2026-11-19 `ignite test fork` after a one-line comment change built three products one after another and took 300 s, of which its output accounted for 130 s)

The landing gate's memory of what a change's last passing gate chose, and of the rate its gates achieved, lives in the daemon's database instead of the process, so `ignite land` finds what `ignite check` chose: both run in verb processes of their own, and on 2026-11-19 the land of a one-card comment change after a passing check spent a fresh budget of 468 billion instructions in 177 s

The landing gate (`ignite check` and `ignite land`) builds every product its listings need while it lists the families that need none, lists families and runs them on threads of their own, and prints `slow` and `took` lines (on 2026-11-19 `ignite check` of a one-card comment change listed 26 families one after another for 137 s, ran them one after another for 123 s and took 273 s, of which its output accounted for 164 s)

The `ignite test <word>` command keeps a local copy of every listing that is never kept for its inputs, such as one whose checks carry digests, so a family whose checks do not hold the word is not listed again (on 2026-11-19 `ignite test quicksilver_gargantuan` after a one-line card comment change took 198 s, 173 s of it waiting for the Beryl 3D build that `b3d-timeline-drift` needs to be listed)

Windows trees on a Dev Drive (ReFS) start from a block-clone copy of the build nearest the tip as APFS trees on macOS do, where before each built every product from nothing (about 950 to 1,400 CPU-seconds each), and Windows Rust builds link with rust-lld and keep only line tables, since PDB files were 6 GB of an 11 GB test build

A rebase gives each file it writes back unchanged its old modification time, and a landing rebased over other commits gates in its ticket tree when that leaves less to build than every free landing tree (on 2026-11-19 the landing of a one-card comment change rebased over Ignite-only commits rebuilt 74 crates for 76 s in a landing tree after `ignite check` had built the change in its ticket tree)

An express landing keeps an earlier express pass when the only files the commits it rebased over share with the change are `[express] inert` ones (the design document and this file), and the express nextest profile leaves out three more tests that set the run's wall time under load (on 2026-11-19 two Ignite landings each ran all four express commands again, 65 s and 71 s, after rebasing over commits that also edited those two files, and the express test run took 26 to 61 s at a load average of 46 to 62 against 18 to 19 s without the three tests)

The hub files one flaky-check ticket per check family and adds each later switched-off check of that family to it as a comment (on 2026-11-19 two `ignite` tests that flaked on one machine within the same hour each got their own ticket and would have each cost a session)

Rust tests that open a repository file through `beryl_test_files` or `ignite_core::test_files` are hashed over the files they were seen to open, so a data file reruns only the tests that opened it, not every test of the package that lists it in `package_inputs`

The `ignite test <word>` command lists a Rust test family for the packages of the tests it names and the packages the branch changes, and every Rust test run selects only its tests' packages, so a card file edit no longer builds every package's test binaries to run one test (on 2026-11-19 `ignite test fork` after a one-line card comment change waited 77 s for 35 crates of the `rust-tests` build)

A card edit no longer compiles `beryl_search`, `beryl_session` and `beryl_cli` in full for the `b3d` product, and the Beryl 3D families find each recording's cards from the pack, rereading only recordings that changed, instead of exporting 450 MB (`ignite test fork` after a comment edit: b3d build 162 to about 20-47 CPU-s, b3d listing 20 s to about 1 s)

The main, Beryl 3D and Ignite workspaces' tests open repository files through the recording helpers, so a change to `data/card-store.tsv`, a card file or the UI conventions reruns only the tests that opened that file, and the `check-inputs` rule fails a raw `std::fs` read of the checkout

The landing gate asks the hub for every family's check record at once and only for the areas its change touches, sends new listings to the hub in the background, and converts its budget at the rate its running stage achieved, so `ignite check` of a one-card change stops spending 85 s planning and four budgets running

A comment edit in one card file no longer recompiles the search crate and everything above it (about 150 CPU-seconds with beryl_session and beryl_cli), because beryl_search takes its card names from a new crate, beryl_card_names, built from the card store alone, and depends on beryl_cards only for its tests

A landing that a daemon restart runs again starts in a new verb process, which outlives the next restart, and the gate remembers the checks it chose as soon as it plans them, not only when it passes, so a landing after failed or cut-off gates of the same change spends no fresh budget (on 2026-11-20 a one-card landing was cut off five times in 13 minutes and ran about 2,100 checks, then its retry ran 1,685 more)

A lease prebuilds the products beside the ticket's files first, so an Ignite ticket's tree has Ignite's test build current before Beryl's, and the express commands compile on every core instead of the 2 reserved on multivac, so an express landing there stops spending 130 to 165 s rebuilding Ignite

A generated crate, `beryl_workspace_hack`, gives every shared dependency the whole Rust workspace's features in a build of any one package, so Ignite builds only the selected packages' test binaries instead of falling back to the whole workspace's (35 crates, 33-77 s) after a card edit

A seed clones each of a donor tree's Cargo profile directories in one `clonefile` call (7 s for 72,000 files under load, against 134-680 s file by file), passes over a donor that is building for the next one, and starts again after a daemon restart, so a leased tree whose build the disk loop deleted no longer compiles about 320 crates from nothing on its first `ignite test`

The `beryl_cli` library takes the cards as a `Catalog` from its binary, now the package `beryl_cli_main`, and Beryl 3D's recorder, so a card file edit relinks those binaries and recompiles none of the library's 20,000 lines, here or in Beryl 3D's build

Ignite's scheduler counts the hub and verb processes outside the daemon's process tree as Ignite's own CPU, not as load outside Ignite, so it hands out the cores they use instead of holding them back from waiting agent commands

The settings, protocol types, trait methods and fakes for landing by verdict and a green branch exist with defaults that change nothing, so the tickets that make `ignite land` take seconds (one gate per tree and base, rebased in git's object database) can be built at the same time against the fakes
The daemon ends a verb process that was asked to stop by any path and still runs 60 seconds later, so a hung check no longer holds its tree and a core for hours

The hub stores and looks up verdicts (one per tree, base and gate settings, kept 30 days), so a change that passed the gate on one machine can later be landed from any machine without running the gate again

Ignite's git client rebases and reverts commits in git's object database (`git merge-tree --write-tree` and `git commit-tree`), leaving the ticket tree's files untouched, so that a landing by verdict can push the rebased commit without recompiling everything that landed since the ticket started (about 25 CPU-minutes per landing on 2026-11-19)

An `ignite check` that passes stores a verdict when its gate passes (keyed by the tree's files, its merge base with the tip and the `[gate]` section, at the hub and in the daemon's local table), so a later landing of the same tree can look the pass up instead of running the gate again

With `repository.green` set, a tip round runs the build checks (clippy, `tsc`, pyre) before its other checks and moves the `green` branch once they pass, so that new work can start from a commit known to compile within minutes of landing instead of after the whole round (median 5.2 minutes, up to 89, on 2026-11-19)
A change to a skill under `.agents/` or `.claude/` no longer puts Ignite's own tests in scope, because `ignite_cli`'s tests do not read those directories

The scheduler keeps a machine's `tip_build_cores` for the build checks of a tip round (`Reserve::TipBuild`), which start at once on them however full the machine is, so `green` and the tickets waiting on it are not held behind a dozen one-core commands, and idle reserved cores are lent to the express lane and the release build

The command `ignite test <name>` leaves out a family whose listing needs a product build when every name it matches is also matched by a family that is cheap to list, and names it on a `skipped` line, and `ignite test fork` after a one-line change to a card file spent 24 to 55 minutes listing two Beryl 3D interface families before running its one Rust test (2026-11-19)

Both `ignite start` and `ignite sync` begin at `green` when `repository.green` is set (a dependency's landed commit that `green` lacks, or the `staging` tip for a regression ticket, being the exceptions), so a new tree does not start at a tip that fails to compile before a tip round reverts it

Tests that name real cards moved out of the kernel, rules, search, session, table and command-line libraries into `tests/` binaries, and the `card-leaves` check keeps card crates out of every non-leaf crate's normal dependencies, so a card edit rebuilds only the leaf crates instead of every crate that depends on `beryl_cards`
With `[revert] broken_build` set, a tip round reverts the one landing that made a build check fail, so agents and tip rounds are not left on a tip that does not compile while a fix is written

With `[land] mode = "verdict"`, a change that touches none of Ignite's own source lands by the verdict its gate earned on its own base: the commits are rebased onto the tip in git's object database and pushed without building or checking again when the tip moves (the slowest gated landing on 2026-11-19 took 91 minutes over 7 passes)
A reverted landing reopens its ticket at P0 and the dispatcher offers it to the session that wrote it, which still has the context, and sessions holding dependent tickets are told to release them

Landing by verdict, the `green` branch, the revert of a landing that breaks the build and the tip-build core reserve are switched on in `ignite.toml`, so a landing checked on its own base no longer rebuilds and gates again each time another landing moves the tip (the slowest gated landing on 2026-11-19 took 91 minutes over 7 passes, none of whose repeats found a failure)

The landing gate lists families without building their products when the change cannot alter their listings: listings of families marked `listing_ignores_comments` hash Rust files without comments, a `nextest` family reuses its newest listing for every package whose own files did not change and builds only the changed packages' tests, and clippy, card-text and three browser families list without waiting for their run products
Beryl 3D frame gates use fixed budgets, so ordinary count changes no longer require measuring and editing exact pins in each commit.
Ignite budgets worktree build growth before handing out tickets and paces new build tickets while the core queue recovers, so active worktrees can keep their build outputs.
The default Beryl 3D interface test runs one recording per distinct signature and keeps every fixture and story
Beryl 3D's text and picture tools read verb tuning at startup, so an edit to a flight arc or another verb value can be previewed without recompiling the client.
Standalone Beryl 3D tests run in the crates they exercise, reducing the app and host suites that need rebuilding for lower-level test edits.
Beryl 3D's inspector reads drawing layers for glow, dissolve and life loss at startup, so changes to these effects can be previewed without recompiling it.
Beryl 3D loads audit, pointer, playback and presentation tuning from the checkout, so editing those values no longer recompiles the inspector or picture tool.
Beryl 3D layout edits can reuse renderer and asset-worker builds because both consume shared atlas records and the host supplies artwork to the worker.
Loading the remaining eleven Beryl 3D effects from data lets the inspector replay changes to all 14 effects without recompiling.
Beryl 3D reloads valid runtime tuning in the running app, so a tuning edit can be checked without restarting and replaying to the same point.
Commands for regressions and master-lag justiciar tickets get shared cores before queued feature work, reducing the wait to verify fixes that hold master back.
Ignite runs checks with recent product catches before landing changes in the culprit's areas, so tip verification has fewer product regressions to repair.
Ignite switches ordinary checks off after one invalid failure and files a remedy, reducing time spent on repeated false alarms.
Beryl 3D landing checks build and test only the corpus recordings and fixtures
The Rust test, scenario and CLI builds share dependency features and use the same compiler settings for build and normal dependencies.
Without nextest, Beryl 3D runs the requested packages' test binaries from the shared workspace build, avoiding a separate build with package-specific dependency features.
Ignite admits ordinary tickets when the build queue is backed up and measured CPU use allows more work.
Ignite lends idle tip and express cores to agent commands and recalls the loans when work arrives for either reserve.
The Beryl 3D map gives agents source and data paths directly from client registries, shortening the search for code to change.
Beryl 3D scaffolds supply the first story, test and registry edits for new client parts, reducing setup time.
Beryl 3D agents read a short workspace guide and the guide for the crate they change, loading web comparison instructions only when needed.
Ignite caps concurrent build tickets by shared scheduler cores to keep overlapping builds from backing up the command queue.
Windows Rust builds share dependency features across workspace tests, package tests, and the CLI and scenario products.
Ignite batches ordinary flaky-check reports so one investigation can use repeated evidence from failures that share a cause.
The engine and Beryl 3D benchmark listings run while the benchmark virtual machine is busy, so reading the list of checks no longer holds up landing checks.
